claim: Participants completed 60 trials of the Trust Game and a matched bandit task while undergoing functional neuroimaging (fMRI).
source: Participants (N=28) completed 60 trials of the Trust Game and a matched bandit task (order counterbalanced), while undergoing functional neuroimaging (fMRI).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design and data collection methods used in the study.

claim: Participants invested more money with the high return social partner compared to the bandit (mean social investment: $7.12; mean bandit investment: $6.43; t=–3.57, p<0.001).
source: Despite being perfectly matched across social and nonsocial conditions, participants invested more money with the high return social partner compared to the bandit (mean social investment: $7.12; mean bandit investment: $6.43; t=–3.57, p<0.001; Figure 2A)
evidence: Statistical comparison of investment amounts between social and nonsocial conditions with t-test results and reference to Figure 2A.

claim: Participants invested less money with the low return partner vs. bandit (mean social investment: $1.71; mean bandit investment: $2.71; t=5.69, p<0.001).
source: and less money with the low return partner vs. bandit (mean social investment: $1.71; mean bandit investment: $2.71; t=5.69, p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical comparison showing differential investment behavior between social and nonsocial conditions for low return stimuli.

claim: No differences in mean investments were observed for the neutral or random stimuli across tasks.
source: No differences in mean investments were observed for the neutral or random stimuli across tasks (all ps >0.1).
evidence: Statistical test results indicating no significant differences for neutral and random stimuli.

claim: The most recently experienced relevant outcome exerted the largest effect on investments.
source: The most recently experienced relevant outcome exerted the largest effect on investments (significant difference between slopes at t-1 vs. t-2: t=–4.98, p<0.001; Figure 2B).
evidence: Statistical comparison of regression slopes showing recency effects with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: A stronger effect of previous outcomes on investments with partners compared to bandits was observed (significant effect at t-1 in which slopes were larger for the social vs. nonsocial task: t=3.19, p=0.004).
source: We also observed a stronger effect of previous outcomes on investments with partners compared to bandits (a significant effect at t-1 in which slopes were larger for the social vs. nonsocial task: t=3.19, p=0.004; Figure 2B).
evidence: Statistical comparison of learning effects between social and nonsocial tasks with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: Recent irrelevant outcomes influenced decisions to gamble with bandits (t=1.83, p=0.039).
source: We observed that recent irrelevant outcomes (mean slope from t-1 through t-3) influenced decisions to gamble with bandits (t=1.83, p=0.039; Figure 2B)
evidence: Statistical test showing effect of irrelevant outcomes on bandit task decisions with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: Recent irrelevant outcomes were anticorrelated with choices to trust partners (t=–2.73, p=0.011).
source: whereas recent irrelevant outcomes were anticorrelated with choices to trust partners (t=–2.73, p=0.011).
evidence: Statistical test showing negative correlation between irrelevant outcomes and trust decisions.

claim: Task differences in using irrelevant prior outcomes to guide choices were significant (t=3.42, p<0.001).
source: These task differences in using irrelevant prior outcomes to guide choices were significant (t=3.42, p<0.001; Figure 2B).
evidence: Statistical comparison of task differences in outcome attribution with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: Prior relevant outcomes that were rewarding exerted a stronger influence on choices compared to losses (t=–4.27, p<0.001).
source: Across tasks, prior relevant outcomes that were rewarding exerted a stronger influence on choices compared to losses (significant difference between slopes for gains versus losses; t=–4.27, p<0.001; Figure 2C).
evidence: Statistical comparison showing valence-dependent learning effects with reference to Figure 2C.

claim: Immediately preceding irrelevant losses disproportionately impacted decisions compared to gains (t=2.21, p=0.029).
source: In contrast, immediately preceding irrelevant losses disproportionately impacted decisions compared to gains (t=2.21, p=0.029; Figure 2C)
evidence: Statistical test showing differential impact of loss vs. gain outcomes with reference to Figure 2C.

claim: Behavior was best fit by the credit assignment model with valenced CA parameters (V-LR, V-CA) in both the trust and bandit task.
source: Behavior was best fit by the credit assignment model with valenced CA parameters (V-LR, V-CA) in both the trust and bandit task (see Methods).
evidence: Model comparison results indicating the best-fitting computational model.

claim: People assigned credit more precisely to partners, and spread credit more diffusely across bandits (trust task mean CA estimate = 0.74; bandit task mean CA estimate = 0.54; F=10.67, p=0.002).
source: Consistent with the behavioral analyses above, our model reveals that people assigned credit more precisely to partners, and spread credit more diffusely across bandits (trust task mean CA estimate = 0.74; bandit task mean CA estimate = 0.54; F=10.67, p=0.002; Figure 3B)
evidence: Model parameter estimates showing task differences in credit assignment precision with statistical test and reference to Figure 3B.

claim: Credit assignment precision was heightened for gains compared to losses (F=4.72, p=0.033).
source: —an effect that was heightened for gains compared to losses (F=4.72, p=0.033; Figure 3C).
evidence: Statistical test showing valence-dependent differences in credit assignment with reference to Figure 3C.

claim: Neural patterns in the mPFC, lOFC, and mOFC met basic criteria for providing state representations at the time of choice.
source: Neural patterns in a constellation of brain regions including the mPFC, lOFC, and mOFC met basic criteria for providing state representations (statistically significant beta coefficients of the identity RDM) at the time of choice (Figure 5B; see Supplementary file 1a for ROI coordinates).
evidence: RSA results showing significant state representations in prefrontal regions with reference to Figure 5B.

claim: Stimulus identity was more strongly encoded in the trust vs. bandit task across ROIs (trust task mean β=0.019; bandit task mean β=0.012; t=–3.64, p<0.001).
source: Within these regions, stimulus' identity was more strongly encoded in the trust vs. bandit task across ROIs (trust task mean β=0.019; bandit task mean β=0.012; t=–3.64, p<0.001; Figure 5B)
evidence: Statistical comparison of neural encoding strength between tasks with reference to Figure 5B.

claim: There was a positive relationship between an individual's mean CA parameter estimates and the strength of the stimulus' identity representation in the PFC ROIs across both tasks (t=3.38, p<0.001).
source: There was also a positive relationship between an individual's mean CA parameter estimates and the strength of the stimulus' identity representation in the PFC ROIs across both tasks (t=3.38, p<0.001; Figure 5C)
evidence: Statistical test showing correlation between credit assignment precision and neural representation fidelity with reference to Figure 5C.

claim: The relationship between CA and neural representation did not depend on outcome valence (CA positive: t=3.26, p=0.0014; CA negative: t=2.50, p=0.014).
source: which did not depend on outcome valence (CA positive: t=3.26, p=0.0014; CA negative: t=2.50, p=0.014)
evidence: Statistical tests showing the relationship holds for both positive and negative outcomes.

claim: The more money earned in the task, the more discriminable stimulus representations were in the PFC ROIs in both tasks (t=4.14, p<.001).
source: Furthermore, the more money earned in the task, the more discriminable these stimulus representations were in the PFC ROIs in both tasks (t=4.14, p<.001).
evidence: Statistical test showing correlation between task earnings and neural representation discriminability.

claim: Stronger identity representations in the trust task were observed in the mPFC at the time of feedback (t=–2.41, p=0.023).
source: We observed stronger identity representations in the trust task in the mPFC (t=–2.41, p=0.023; the fidelity of state representations did not differ across tasks in any additional ROIs).
evidence: Statistical test showing task differences in mPFC state encoding during feedback.

claim: Stronger identity encoding during positive vs. negative PE trials was observed in the mPFC (main effect of valence: F=4.33, p=0.039).
source: Across tasks we observed stronger identity encoding during positive vs. negative PE trials in the mPFC (main effect of valence: F=4.33, p=0.039; Figure 5E)
evidence: Statistical test showing valence effects on state encoding in mPFC with reference to Figure 5E.

claim: Stronger identity encoding during positive vs. negative PE trials was observed in the lOFC (F=5.98, p=0.017).
evidence: Statistical test showing valence effects on state encoding in lOFC.

claim: The valence effect on state encoding was significantly greater in the trust compared to bandit task (t=–2.71, p=0.008).
source: an effect that was significantly greater in the trust compared to bandit task (t=–2.71, p=0.008).
evidence: Statistical test showing task differences in valence-dependent state encoding.

claim: A significant positive relationship was observed between an individual's credit assignment precision (CA parameters) and the consistency of their representations of the stimulus across both timepoints in the mPFC and lOFC (pooled estimate across ROIs: t=2.17, p=0.033).
source: Across both tasks, we observed a significant positive relationship between an individual's credit assignment precision (CA parameters) and the consistency of their representations of the stimulus across both timepoints in the mPFC and lOFC (pooled estimate across ROIs: t=2.17, p=0.033; Figure 6C; see Supplementary file 1c for ROI coordinates)
evidence: Statistical test showing correlation between credit assignment and cross-timepoint neural consistency with reference to Figure 6C.

claim: The relationship between CA and cross-timepoint consistency was selectively enhanced for gains but not losses (t=3.48, p<0.001).
source: —an effect that was selectively enhanced for gains but not losses (t=3.48, p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical test showing valence-specific effects on the relationship between CA and neural consistency.

claim: Significant clusters of PE modulation were observed in the ventral striatum and ventral medial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC).
source: A task-summed t-map revealed significant clusters in the ventral striatum and ventral medial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC; corrected for multiple comparisons; Figure 7A; see Supplementary file 1d for ROI coordinates).
evidence: Whole brain parametric modulation analysis results with reference to Figure 7A.

claim: The strength of PE signaling did not differ across the trust and bandit tasks in the ventral striatum and vmPFC regions.
source: Critically, the strength of PE signaling did not differ across the trust and bandit tasks in these regions (all ps >0.1; Figure 7B), even at a lowered threshold (p<0.001 uncorrected).
evidence: Statistical tests showing no task differences in PE signaling with reference to Figure 7B.

claim: The effect of CA on stimulus representation during choice was significant even when controlling for the learning rate (t=3.31, p<0.0012).
source: The effect of CA on stimulus representation was significant even when controlling for the learning rate (choice: t=3.31, p<0.0012, cross-timepoint: t=2.11, p=0.036; both LR and CA were included as additive terms predicting choice and cross-timepoint beta coefficients for state representation)
evidence: Statistical test showing CA effects remain significant after controlling for learning rate.

claim: The effect of CA on cross-timepoint stimulus representation was significant even when controlling for the learning rate (t=2.11, p=0.036).
source: The effect of CA on stimulus representation was significant even when controlling for the learning rate (choice: t=3.31, p<0.0012, cross-timepoint: t=2.11, p=0.036; both LR and CA were included as additive terms predicting choice and cross-timepoint beta coefficients for state representation)
evidence: Statistical test showing CA effects on cross-timepoint representation remain significant after controlling for learning rate.

claim: Learning rate was not significant in predicting choice or cross-timepoint state representation (all ps >0.09).
source: and LR was not significant in either model (all ps >0.09).
evidence: Statistical tests showing learning rate does not predict neural state representations.

claim: Data was collected from 30 right-handed adults (ages 21–36; mean age = 23.5, Nfemale = 16) in the Providence, Rhode Island area.
source: Data was collected from 30 right-handed adults (ages 21–36; mean age = 23.5, Nfemale = 16) in the Providence, Rhode Island area.
evidence: Direct statement of participant demographics and sample characteristics.

claim: Two participants were removed from the final sample due to a high degree of motion artifacts (movement >3 mm).
source: After all fMRI preprocessing steps were completed, two participants were removed from the final sample due a high degree of motion artifacts (movement >3 mm).
evidence: Statement of data exclusion criteria and resulting sample size.

claim: The study protocol was approved by Brown University's Institutional Review Board (Protocol #1607001555).
source: Our study protocol was approved by Brown University's Institutional Review Board (Protocol #1607001555) and all participants indicated informed consent before completing the social and the bandit tasks in the scanner.
evidence: Statement of ethical approval for the research.

claim: All participants indicated informed consent before completing the social and the bandit tasks in the scanner.
source: Our study protocol was approved by Brown University's Institutional Review Board (Protocol #1607001555) and all participants indicated informed consent before completing the social and the bandit tasks in the scanner.
evidence: Statement of informed consent procedures.

claim: All participants received monetary compensation ($15/hour) and additional performance-based bonus payment of up to $20.
source: All participants received monetary compensation ($15 /hour) and additional performance-based bonus payment of up to $20.
evidence: Statement of participant compensation.

claim: Face stimuli were drawn from the MR2 database.
source: In reality, each of the four face stimuli were drawn from the MR2 database (Strohminger et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement of stimulus source with citation.

claim: All face stimuli included in the task were prejudged to be equivalent on trustworthiness and attractiveness dimensions by independent raters.
source: All face stimuli included in our task were prejudged to be equivalent on trustworthiness and attractiveness dimensions by independent raters (Strohminger et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement of stimulus validation with citation.

claim: Each trial was designed to elapse over a 16 s duration.
source: Each trial was designed to elapse over a 16 s duration.
evidence: Statement of experimental timing parameters.

claim: The trial was initiated with a choice phase with a 3 s response window in which participants indicated their investment using a 5-button response box.
source: The trial was initiated with a choice phase with a 3 s response window in which participants indicated their investment using a 5-button response box (options: $0, $2.50, $5.00, $7.50, $10.00).
evidence: Statement of experimental procedure and response options.

claim: After participants keyed in their response, a jittered interstimulus interval (ITI), randomly distributed between 1 and 5 s, reminded participants of their investment.
source: After participants keyed in their response, a jittered interstimulus interval (ITI), randomly distributed between 1 and 5 s, reminded participants of their investment.
evidence: Statement of experimental timing and procedure.

claim: The outcome was presented for a fixed 2 s duration.
source: The outcome was then presented for a fixed 2 s duration, following by an additional ITI, filled with however many seconds remained for the full 16 s trial duration (between 6 and 13 s).
evidence: Statement of experimental timing parameters.

claim: If participants failed to indicate their investment within the 3 s response window, the investment was considered $0.
source: If participants failed to indicate their investment within the 3 s response window, the investment was considered $0, and a missed trial prompt appeared during the ITI.
evidence: Statement of experimental procedure for missed responses.

claim: Missed trials were omitted from all behavioral and RSA analyses.
source: Missed trials were omitted from all behavioral and RSA analyses.
evidence: Statement of data analysis exclusion criteria.

claim: Stimulus ordering was randomly interleaved, and consecutive presentations of the same stimulus could occur anywhere from 1 to 15 trials apart following a right-skewed distribution.
source: Stimulus ordering was randomly interleaved, and therefore consecutive presentations of the same stimulus could occur anywhere from 1 to 15 trials apart following a right-skewed distribution, such that most consecutive stimulus interactions occurred within 1–5 trials.
evidence: Statement of experimental design for stimulus presentation.

claim: Each stimulus in the social and bandit tasks was randomly assigned to follow one of four reward distributions.
source: Each stimulus in the social and bandit tasks was randomly assigned to follow one of four reward distributions, such that stimulus identities were counterbalanced across different payoff structures.
evidence: Statement of experimental design for reward structure.

claim: The high reward stimulus always returned more than the participant initially invested and thus always resulted in a net gain.
source: The high reward stimulus always returned more than the participant initially invested and thus always resulted in a net gain, whereas the low reward stimulus always returned a lower amount resulting in a net loss.
evidence: Statement of reward structure design.

claim: The low reward stimulus always returned a lower amount resulting in a net loss.
source: The high reward stimulus always returned more than the participant initially invested and thus always resulted in a net gain, whereas the low reward stimulus always returned a lower amount resulting in a net loss.
evidence: Statement of reward structure design.

claim: Neutral and random stimuli were designed to return a roughly equivalent amount and served as a control for outcome valence.
source: Neutral and random stimuli were designed to return a roughly equivalent amount and served as a control for outcome valence, allowing us to examine outcome attribution precision with stimuli that resulted in net gains and losses with equal frequency.
evidence: Statement of experimental design rationale for control conditions.

claim: Neutral and random stimuli only differed in terms of their return variance (i.e. the extremity of gains and losses).
source: Neutral and random stimuli only differed in terms of their return variance (i.e. the extremity of gains and losses).
evidence: Statement of experimental design distinguishing control conditions.

claim: Return rates were preselected so that the full range of the distribution was sampled from, rather than truly sampling from a payoff distribution.
source: Rather than truly sampling from a payoff distribution which could have resulted in vastly different observed outcomes across participants and tasks (e.g. observing a consistent string of gains or losses on the extreme end of the distribution simply due to chance), we preselected the return rates so that the full range of the distribution was sampled from.
evidence: Statement of experimental design decision and rationale.

claim: Preselected return rates were applied for all participants and in each task but their ordering was randomized across trials.
source: We then applied these preselected return rates for all participants and in each task but allowed their ordering to be randomized across trials.
evidence: Statement of experimental design for outcome presentation.

claim: The payoff on each trial was still dependent on the participant's investment despite fixed return rates.
source: Notably, although return rates were fixed, the payoff on each trial was still dependent on the participant's investment (see task structure in Figure 1).
evidence: Statement of task mechanics with reference to Figure 1.

claim: Investment data for each participant was modeled separately including both social and bandit tasks in the same linear regression model.
source: To capture individual learning effects, we modeled investment data for each participant separately including both social and bandit tasks in the same linear regression model.
evidence: Statement of statistical analysis approach.

claim: Investments were modeled as a weighted sum of previous returns experienced on relevant trials as well as irrelevant trials.
source: Investments were modeled as a weighted sum of previous returns experienced on relevant trials (i.e. those with a matched stimulus) as well as irrelevant trials (i.e. those that immediately preceded a given investment, irrespective of stimulus identity).
evidence: Statement of regression model structure.

claim: Four separate regression models were run quantifying the effects of lag1 returns for each combination of relevant vs. irrelevant and gain vs. loss trials.
source: Here we considered only lag1 trials to minimize parameter tradeoffs that prevented model convergence, and furthermore ran four separate regression models quantifying the effects of lag1 returns for each combination of relevant vs. irrelevant and gain vs. loss trials.
evidence: Statement of statistical analysis approach for valence effects.

claim: Choices in the task were both discrete and ordinal in their magnitude (choice options: $0, $2.50, $5.00, $7.50, $10.00).
source: Because choices in the task were both discrete and ordinal in their magnitude (choice options: $0, $2.50, $5.00, $7.50, $10.00), we used a logistic function to model the learned value of investing with each partner/bandit type based on trial and error.
evidence: Statement of task design and modeling rationale.

claim: A logistic function was used to model the learned value of investing with each partner/bandit type based on trial and error.
source: Because choices in the task were both discrete and ordinal in their magnitude (choice options: $0, $2.50, $5.00, $7.50, $10.00), we used a logistic function to model the learned value of investing with each partner/bandit type based on trial and error.
evidence: Statement of computational modeling approach.

claim: All choices in which the participant responded were included in model fitting.
source: In each of our models, all choices in which the participant responded were included in model fitting.
evidence: Statement of data inclusion criteria for modeling.

claim: The width of the Gaussian distribution was fixed to a value of 1 in all models.
source: The width of the Gaussian distribution was fixed to a value of 1 in all models, controlling the variability in model investments.
evidence: Statement of model parameter constraint.

claim: The model was fit by minimizing the negative log of the sum of p(investments) corresponding to the actual participant investments across trials.
source: and the model was fit by minimizing the negative log of the sum of p(investments) corresponding to the actual participant investments across trials.
evidence: Statement of model fitting procedure.

claim: A learning model was fit to behavior separately for social and bandit tasks.
source: We fit a learning model to behavior separately for social and bandit tasks.
evidence: Statement of modeling approach.

claim: A matrix was used to store the updated value of V on each trial separately for each stimulus, resulting in a trial × stimulus V matrix for each participant and each task.
source: We used a matrix to store the updated value of V on each trial separately for each stimulus, resulting in a trial × stimulus V matrix for each participant and each task.
evidence: Statement of computational implementation.

claim: In the baseline model, outcomes were always attributed to the appropriate state (i.e. updated V for only the appropriate stimulus), effectively performing standard model-free RL.
source: In the baseline model, outcomes were always attributed to the appropriate state (i.e. updated V for only the appropriate stimulus), effectively performing standard model-free RL.
evidence: Statement of baseline model assumptions.

claim: Model fits were evaluated using the Akaike information criterion (AIC).
source: Model fits were then evaluated using the Akaike information criterion (AIC), which we computed as:
evidence: Statement of model comparison method.

claim: Model selection was performed by maximizing the negative AIC and minimizing Δ AIC.
source: We performed model selection by maximizing the negative AIC and minimizing Δ AIC, which was calculated as the difference between each participant's best-fitting model and every other model in the set.
evidence: Statement of model selection procedure.

claim: Model comparison was performed separately for social and bandit tasks.
source: Model comparison was performed separately for social and bandit tasks (see Supplementary file 1g-1h and Figure 3—figure supplement 2 for AIC and Δ AIC values of each model).
evidence: Statement of model comparison approach with reference to supplementary materials.

claim: Model confusability was evaluated by simulating 100 participants per model.
source: Model confusability was evaluated by simulating 100 participants per model.
evidence: Statement of model validation procedure.

claim: For each simulated participant, free parameters were randomly sampled from a uniform distribution and trial-to-trial investments were generated under the sampled parameterization.
source: For each simulated participant, free parameters were randomly sampled from a uniform distribution and trial-to-trial investments were generated under the sampled parameterization.
evidence: Statement of simulation procedure for model validation.

claim: Each model was fit to each simulated participant using 20 iterations of gradient descent.
source: Each model was fit to each simulated participant using 20 iterations of gradient descent, and classification rates were computed as the frequency with which each participant was best fit by the correct generative model, which we evaluated by maximizing the negative AIC (rate of winning model/true model; see Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Statement of model fitting procedure for validation with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: Data was acquired at the Brown University MRI Facility with the Siemens Prisma 3T MRI Scanner.
source: Data was acquired at the Brown University MRI Facility with the Siemens Prisma 3T MRI Scanner.
evidence: Statement of data acquisition equipment and location.

claim: Anatomical scans were collected using a T1-weighted sequence with 1 mm3 isotropic voxels, 1900ms TR, flip angle = 9 degrees, 160 slices/volume, 1 mm slice thickness, for a duration of 4 min, 1 s.
source: Anatomical scans were collected using a T1-weighted sequence with 1 mm3 isotropic voxels, 1900ms TR, flip angle = 9 degrees, 160 slices/volume, 1 mm slice thickness, for a duration of 4 min, 1 s.
evidence: Statement of MRI acquisition parameters for anatomical scans.

claim: Functional scans were acquired using a T2-weighted sequence with 3 mm3 isotropic voxels, 2000ms TR, flip angle = 78 degrees, 38 slices/volume, 3 mm slice thickness.
source: Functional scans were acquired using a T2-weighted sequence with 3 mm3 isotropic voxels, 2000ms TR, flip angle = 78 degrees, 38 slices/volume, 3 mm slice thickness.
evidence: Statement of MRI acquisition parameters for functional scans.

claim: Each task was divided into 2 functional runs, each consisting of 246 volumes, for a duration of 8 min and 12 s.
source: Each task was divided into 2 functional runs, each consisting of 246 volumes, for a duration of 8 min and 12 s.
evidence: Statement of fMRI data acquisition structure.

claim: A bounding box with a forward tilt along the AC-PC axis was used to ensure imaging of lateral and medial OFC.
source: We used a bounding box with a forward tilt along the AC-PC axis to ensure we were imaging lateral and medial OFC.
evidence: Statement of MRI acquisition parameters for specific brain regions.

claim: Data was preprocessed in SPM12.
source: Data was preprocessed in SPM12.
evidence: Statement of preprocessing software.

claim: For multivariate analyses, data was preprocessed in the following sequence: slice-time correction, realignment, co-registration, segmentation, normalization, spatial smoothing.
source: For multivariate analyses, data was preprocessed in the following sequence: slice-time correction, realignment, co-registration, segmentation, normalization, spatial smoothing.
evidence: Statement of preprocessing pipeline for multivariate analyses.

claim: Images were normalized to a standard MNI template and resampled to 2 mm3 voxels.
source: Images were normalized to a standard MNI template and resampled to 2 mm3 voxels.
evidence: Statement of normalization procedure.

claim: For univariate parametric modulation analyses, images were realigned prior to slice-time correction.
source: For univariate parametric modulation analyses, we used the same preprocessing sequence, except images were realigned prior to slice-time correction.
evidence: Statement of preprocessing pipeline modification for univariate analyses.

claim: Images were smoothed using a 2 mm3 smoothing kernel for multivariate analyses and with an 8 mm3 kernel for univariate analyses.
source: Images were smoothed using a 2 mm3 smoothing kernel for multivariate analyses and with an 8 mm3 kernel for univariate analyses.
evidence: Statement of smoothing parameters for different analysis types.

claim: RSA images constructed from the deconvolved time-series GLM were smoothed using a 6 mm3 smoothing kernel for group analyses.
source: RSA images constructed from the deconvolved time-series GLM (see below) were later smoothed using a 6 mm3 smoothing kernel for group analyses.
evidence: Statement of smoothing parameters for RSA group analyses.

claim: Time-series estimates of the BOLD signal were obtained by deconvolving the HRF using single trial regressors.
source: For each participant we obtained time-series estimates of the BOLD signal by deconvolving the HRF using single trial regressors (Mumford and Poldrack, 2007; Ramsey et al., 2010), concatenated across task runs.
evidence: Statement of GLM approach with citations to methodological papers.

claim: Separate trial regressors for choice and feedback onsets were included within each GLM.
source: We also included separate trial regressors for choice and feedback onsets within each GLM (i.e., choice and feedback onsets were modeled simultaneously) to control for potential temporal correlations in the BOLD signal resulting from consecutive task events.
evidence: Statement of GLM design to control for temporal correlations.

claim: For choice phase regressors, voxel activations were modeled during the choice duration, which occurred within a 3 s window.
source: For choice phase regressors, we modeled voxel activations during the choice duration, which occurred within a 3 s window.
evidence: Statement of GLM regressor timing.

claim: Feedback phase activations were modeled during a fixed 2 s duration.
source: Feedback phase activations were modeled during a fixed 2 s duration.
evidence: Statement of GLM regressor timing.

claim: Six motion regressors derived from realignment were included along roll, pitch, yaw and x,y,z dimensions to control for motion artifact.
source: We included six motions regressors derived from realignment, along roll, pitch, yaw and x,y,z dimensions to control for motion artifact.
evidence: Statement of motion correction procedure.

claim: Additional framewise displacement (FD) regressors were included, using a FD threshold = 1.2 to identify noisy images.
source: We also included additional framewise displacement (FD) regressors, using a FD threshold = 1.2 to identify noisy images.
evidence: Statement of motion artifact identification procedure.

claim: Noise was regressed out from frames above the FD threshold, including the previous images and subsequent two images.
source: We then regressed out noise from frames above the FD threshold, including the previous images and subsequent two images, based on recommendations (Power et al., 2012; Power et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement of motion artifact correction procedure with citations.

claim: Four independent searchlight analyses were conducted across the whole brain to measure representational dissimilarity during choice and feedback phases of the task, separately for social and bandit tasks.
source: We conducted four independent searchlight analyses across the whole brain to measure representational dissimilarity during choice and feedback phases of the task, and separately for social and bandit tasks.
evidence: Statement of RSA analysis approach.

claim: A 9 mm radius spherical searchlight was constructed and moved along x,y,z coordinates of participant-specific brain masks with a step size of 1.
source: We then constructed a 9 mm radius spherical searchlight, which we moved along x,y,z coordinates of participant-specific brain masks (binary mask of voxels with sufficient accompanying BOLD activations), with a step size of 1, such that the center of the searchlight was placed in each voxel once.
evidence: Statement of searchlight analysis parameters.

claim: Single event beta coefficients from all voxels within the searchlight were extracted from the relevant phase regressors and noise normalized.
source: We then extracted single event (choice/feedback) beta coefficients from all voxels within the searchlight from the relevant phase regressors modeled in our deconvolved time-series GLM and noise normalized the coefficients (Walther et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement of data extraction and normalization procedure with citation.

claim: Beta coefficients from each phase regressor were reorganized into a voxel by trial coefficient matrix.
source: Beta coefficients from each phase regressor were then extracted and reorganized into a voxel by trial coefficient matrix (Figure 4A).
evidence: Statement of data organization procedure with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: The coefficient matrix was reorganized by nesting trial within each stimulus type to align the searchlight neural RDM with the state identity hypothesis matrix.
source: To align the searchlight neural RDM with our state identity hypothesis matrix, we reorganized the coefficient matrix by nesting trial within each stimulus type.
evidence: Statement of data organization for RSA.

claim: The correlation distance (1 r) was computed between each row and column element in the coefficient matrix to obtain the searchlight RDM.
source: To obtain the searchlight RDM, we then computed the correlation distance (1 r) between each row and column element in the coefficient matrix.
evidence: Statement of RDM computation method.

claim: Correlation distance values from the lower triangle of the neural RDM were z-transformed and correlated with the lower triangle of z-transformed predictors.
source: Correlation distance values from the lower triangle (all elements off the identity line) of our neural RDM were then z-transformed and correlated with the lower triangle of our z-transformed predictors, using the following linear model to obtain a t-statistic estimating the effect of state identity for each searchlight (neural correlation distance ~state identity +autocorrelation term).
evidence: Statement of statistical analysis procedure for RSA.

claim: The effect of the state identity and expected value hypothesis matrices were examined separately in whole brain searchlight analyses to avoid systematic correlations from predictor collinearity.
source: We examined the effect of the state identity and expected value hypothesis matrices separately in our whole brain searchlight analyses to avoid any systematic correlations that could potentially emerge from predictor collinearity but allowed state identity and expected value predictors to compete in our ROI analyses.
evidence: Statement of analysis strategy to avoid collinearity issues.

claim: First-level t-maps from the whole brain searchlights for choice and feedback and for each task were spatially smoothed with a 6 mm3 Gaussian smoothing kernel before being submitted to second-level analyses.
source: The resulting first-level t-maps from the whole brain searchlights for choice and feedback and for each task were then spatially smoothed with a 6 mm3 Gaussian smoothing kernel before being submitted to second-level analyses.
evidence: Statement of smoothing procedure for group-level analyses.

claim: Task-combined t-maps were created from each participant's social and bandit searchlights using SPM's imcalc function to avoid constructing task-biased ROIs.
source: To avoid constructing task-biased ROIs, we created summed t-maps from each participant's social and bandit searchlights using SPM's imcalc function (images created using a simple summation method; social t-map +bandit t-map).
evidence: Statement of ROI construction strategy to avoid bias.

claim: Non-parametric permutation testing was conducted on the second-level analyses, using a cluster-forming threshold of p<0.0001 and a null distribution based on 5000 permutations.
source: To correct for multiple comparisons, we conducted non-parametric permutation testing on the second-level analyses, using a cluster-forming threshold of p<0.0001 and a null distribution based on 5000 permutations.
evidence: Statement of multiple comparisons correction procedure.

claim: Permutation testing was conducted with the SnPM package.
source: Permutation testing was conducted with the SnPM package (Hayasaka and Nichols, 2003).
evidence: Statement of software used for permutation testing with citation.

claim: Binary masks were created of all voxels in second-level analyses that were significant at the cluster-level (pFWE <.05) and at the peak level (p<0.0001).
source: We then created binary masks of all voxels in our second-level analyses that were significant at the cluster-level (pFWE <.05) and at the peak level (p<0.0001) and used the task-combined corrected t-maps to identify ROIs.
evidence: Statement of ROI identification criteria.

claim: A data driven approach was used to identify two sets of ROIs for choice and feedback by extracting coefficients from statistically significant cluster peaks in corrected t-maps.
source: We used a data driven approach to identify two sets of ROIs for choice and feedback by extracting coefficients from statistically significant cluster peaks in corrected t-maps.
evidence: Statement of ROI identification approach.

claim: The cluster size of ROIs was limited to be no larger than the size of the searchlight by placing a 9 mm radius sphere at the center of the local maxima.
source: We limited the cluster size of our ROIs to be no larger than the size our searchlight by placing a 9 mm radius sphere at the center of the local maxima and extracted all voxels from the sphere that survived permutation testing.
evidence: Statement of ROI size constraint.

claim: Trial-level deltas (PEs) estimated from the valenced-ca model using the MLE optimized parameters were z-scored for valence-based RSA.
source: For each participant, trial-level deltas (PEs) estimated from the valenced-ca model using the MLE optimized parameters were z-scored to control for the extremity of experienced gains and losses across participants, to ensure we had sufficient trials from each stimulus within both positive and negative valence RDMs, and to ensure a roughly equivalent amount of data in each neural RDM.
evidence: Statement of data normalization procedure for valence-based analysis.

claim: Z-transformed PEs were used to separate data into the appropriate RDM and the RSA procedure for each ROI was separately applied for positive and negative RDMs and for choice and feedback phases.
source: The z-transformed PEs were then used to separate data into the appropriate RDM and our RSA procedure for each ROI was then separately applied for positive and negative RDMs and for choice and feedback phases.
evidence: Statement of valence-specific RSA analysis procedure.

claim: A set of ROIs was constructed in candidate areas that were involved in state representation during both choice and feedback prior to computing cross-timepoint correlations.
source: Prior to computing the cross-timepoint correlations across task phases, we constructed a set of ROIs in candidate areas that were involved in state representation during both choice and feedback.
evidence: Statement of ROI construction for cross-timepoint analysis.

claim: Task and phase-combined t-maps were integrated and masked using a binary conjunction t-map of voxels that survived permutation testing in both choice and feedback phase analyses.
source: To avoid constructing ROIs that were biased towards a particular task phase, we integrated task-combined t-maps (choice t-map +feedback t-map). We then masked our task and phase-combined image using a binary conjunction t-map of voxels that survived permutation testing in both our choice and feedback phase analyses, using a 9 mm radius sphere centered at the local peaks to isolate voxels from statistically significant clusters and focusing specifically on voxels in the PFC.
evidence: Statement of conjunction analysis procedure for cross-timepoint ROIs.

claim: Cross-timepoint correlation was computed within each conjunction ROI, separately for each task.
source: We then computed the cross-timepoint correlation within each of our conjunction ROIs, separately for each task.
evidence: Statement of cross-timepoint analysis procedure.

claim: Two data sets were created for each participant by separating the data into even and odd trials that occurred with each partner/bandit type to compute cross-timepoint correlation.
source: Our approach for computing the cross-timepoint correlation was to first create two data sets for each participant by separating the data into even and odd trials that occurred with each partner/bandit type (e.g. set 1: all even trials with low, high, neutral, random stimuli, set 2: all odd trials with low, high, neutral, random stimuli), so that representational correspondence could be measured across consecutive stimulus-matched trials that were temporally distanced in time (trial ordering was interleaved such that stimulus-matched trials were always 1–15 trials apart in the task; Figure 1D).
evidence: Statement of data splitting procedure for cross-timepoint analysis with reference to Figure 1D.

claim: A data matrix was constructed for each of the even and odd data sets, including choice and feedback in same matrix.
source: We then constructed a data matrix for each of our even and odd data sets, including choice and feedback in same matrix.
evidence: Statement of data organization for cross-timepoint analysis.

claim: Beta coefficients were extracted from each voxel on each trial within even and odd data sets, and concatenated choice and feedback patterns.
source: For each matrix, we extracted beta coefficients from each voxel on each trial within even and odd data sets, and concatenated choice and feedback patterns.
evidence: Statement of data extraction procedure.

claim: Beta coefficients in each voxel were averaged for both even and odd data sets, resulting in two voxel × stimulus matrices reflecting the average beta in each voxel at choice and feedback timepoints.
source: For both even and odd data sets, we then averaged beta coefficients in each voxel, resulting in two voxel × stimulus matrices reflecting the average beta in each voxel at choice and feedback timepoints (rows) and activations for each stimulus during choice and feedback (columns).
evidence: Statement of data averaging procedure.

claim: The correlation distance (1 r) was calculated between even and odd matrices.
source: We then calculated the correlation distance (1 r) between even and odd matrices.
evidence: Statement of cross-timepoint correlation computation.

claim: The matrix product of even and odd RDMs allowed evaluation of the shared structure of state representations across task phases and across independent trials.
source: The resulting matrix product of even and odd RDMs thus allowed us to evaluate the shared structure of state representations across task phases (the lower left and upper right quadrants of the cross-timepoint RDM; Figure 6A) and across independent trials, therefore breaking any systematic temporal or autocorrelation signals within the neural pattern.
evidence: Statement of cross-timepoint analysis rationale with reference to Figure 6A.

claim: Only the cross-timepoint quadrants of the matrix product were correlated with a cross-timepoint state identity matrix to quantify the degree of representational alignment in the neural code across choice and feedback timepoints.
source: We then correlated only the cross-timepoint quadrants of the matrix product with a cross-timepoint state identity matrix to quantify the degree of representational alignment in the neural code across choice and feedback timepoints that preserved the state identity.
evidence: Statement of statistical analysis for cross-timepoint representation.

claim: The degree of shared information in the neural code was submitted to further regression analyses to evaluate the association between shared representational geometry and credit assignment precision.
source: The degree of shared information in the neural code (quantified as Pearson correlation coefficients) was subsequently submitted to further regression analyses to evaluate the association between shared representational geometry and credit assignment precision (Figure 6C).
evidence: Statement of statistical analysis linking neural and behavioral measures with reference to Figure 6C.

claim: ROIs were constructed in the mPFC and lOFC, given that clusters in these regions emerged from the conjunction t-map and signaled cross-timepoint state encoding.
source: We constructed ROIs in the mPFC and lOFC, given that clusters in these regions emerged from our conjunction t-map and signaled cross-timepoint state encoding.
evidence: Statement of ROI selection rationale based on conjunction analysis results.

claim: Univariate parametric modulation analysis was conducted to evaluate the effect of trial PEs on the amplitude of the BOLD signal.
source: We conducted univariate parametric modulation analysis to evaluate the effect of trial PEs on the amplitude of the BOLD signal, allowing us to capture differences in the strength of PE coding across tasks.
evidence: Statement of univariate analysis purpose.

claim: A first-level design matrix was constructed that included regressors for both choice and feedback onsets and durations, and trial-level PEs from the V-LR, V-CA model.
source: For each participant, we constructed a first-level design matrix that included regressors for both choice and feedback onsets and durations, and trial-level PEs from our V-LR, V-CA model.
evidence: Statement of GLM design for parametric modulation analysis.

claim: Social and bandit task data were modeled in the same GLM for parametric modulation analysis.
source: Social and bandit task data were modeled in the same GLM, and we included additional regressors for motion (see time-series GLM section).
evidence: Statement of GLM design combining tasks.

claim: A t-contrast against 0 for the PE regressor was generated in group analyses, including data from both social and bandit tasks.
source: In group analyses we then generated a t-contrast against 0 for the PE regressor. This contrast included data from both social and bandit tasks so that we were blinded to task condition when selecting ROIs.
evidence: Statement of group-level contrast and ROI selection strategy to avoid bias.

claim: Permutation testing was performed on the task-combined t-map to correct for multiple comparisons.
source: To correct for multiple comparisons, we performed permutation testing on the task-combined t-map (see procedure in the whole brain searchlight analysis section).
evidence: Statement of multiple comparisons correction for parametric modulation analysis.

claim: ROIs were selected from significant cluster peaks that survived permutation testing and beta coefficients were extracted from ROIs separately for social and bandit tasks.
source: We then selected ROIs from significant cluster peaks that survived permutation testing and extracted beta coefficients from ROIs separately for social and bandit tasks.
evidence: Statement of ROI selection and data extraction for task comparison.

claim: The PFC serves as a hub for credit assignment by leveraging reward signals and organizing state representations into a shared neural code.
source: Put simply, the PFC serves as a hub for credit assignment by leveraging reward signals and organizing state representations into a shared neural code, allowing for the efficient transfer of credit from feedback to subsequent choice.
evidence: Summary statement of main findings integrating multiple results.

claim: The functional coordination between distinct phases of learning aligns with prior work demonstrating that lOFC and mPFC track task states.
source: This functional coordination between distinct phases of learning aligns with prior work demonstrating that lOFC and mPFC track task states (Schuck et al., 2016), particularly those that govern the structure of rewards, so that humans can respond flexibly and adaptively to shifting environmental demands (Jocham et al., 2016; Nassar et al., 2019; Witkowski et al., 2022).
evidence: Statement connecting current findings to prior literature with multiple citations.

claim: No studies that we are aware of have documented asymmetrical effects of PE valence driving the precision of credit assignment.
source: Although past studies offer insight into credit assignment for rewards (Asaad et al., 2017; Hamid et al., 2021; Jocham et al., 2016; Walton et al., 2010), no studies that we are aware of have documented asymmetrical effects of PE valence driving the precision of credit assignment.
evidence: Statement of novelty of findings with citations to related work.

claim: These results offer an interesting parallel to existing stimulus generalization theories.
source: Thus, these results offer an interesting parallel to existing stimulus generalization theories.
evidence: Statement connecting findings to broader theoretical framework.

claim: Prior work using classical conditioning paradigms shows that the conditioned response is also evoked by novel stimuli.
source: Prior work using classical conditioning paradigms, in which a neutral stimulus is paired with an aversive outcome, shows that the conditioned response is also evoked by novel stimuli (Dunsmoor and Paz, 2015; Hull, 1943; Schechtman et al., 2010).
evidence: Statement of prior findings with citations.

claim: Transfer effects to a new stimulus follows a generalization gradient in which the experienced intensity of the prior aversive outcome predicts increased threat generalization.
source: Transfer effects to a new stimulus follows a generalization gradient in which the experienced intensity of the prior aversive outcome predicts increased threat generalization (Dunsmoor et al., 2017; Lissek et al., 2005), and greater perceptual generalization (Davis et al., 2010; FeldmanHall et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement of prior findings with citations.

claim: The paradigm articulates generalization through credit spreading mechanisms.
source: Although our paradigm articulates generalization through credit spreading mechanisms, from a signal detection standpoint, these findings undoubtedly dovetail with that notion that it is 'better to be safe than sorry' in the aversive domain (Dunsmoor and Paz, 2015).
evidence: Statement connecting current paradigm to theoretical framework with citation.

claim: Increased credit spreading of negative PEs across irrelevant cues can become pathological and maladaptive, offering potential inroads into understanding the etiology of generalized anxiety disorders.
source: This may help to explain why increased credit spreading of negative PEs across irrelevant cues can become pathological and maladaptive, offering potential inroads into understanding the etiology of generalized anxiety disorders.
evidence: Speculative statement about clinical implications of findings.

claim: The study did not control for the visual complexity of the stimuli across tasks (i.e. human faces compared to colored bandits).
source: First, our study did not control for the visual complexity of the stimuli across tasks (i.e. human faces compared to colored bandits).
evidence: Statement of study limitation.

claim: It is unlikely that observed differences in learning and state decoding reflects the salience of faces in the trust task, given that prior work with matched stimulus complexity still observed faster learning in the social domain.
source: While it is possible that the observed differences in learning and state decoding reflects the salience of faces in the trust task, our prior work suggests that this account is unlikely, given that when the stimuli's complexity was perfectly matched across social and nonsocial tasks, we still observe faster learning in the social domain (Lamba et al., 2020).
evidence: Statement addressing potential confound with citation to prior work.

claim: Recent work in mice finds that wave-like dopamine signals from the dorsal striatum communicate when successful actions performed during instrumental learning are necessary for performance.
source: Recent work in mice finds that wave-like dopamine signals from the dorsal striatum communicate when successful actions performed during instrumental learning are necessary for performance, offering insight into the underlying neuromodulatory dynamics of credit assignment in the reward domain (Hamid et al., 2021).
evidence: Statement of prior findings with citation.

claim: Prior work suggests that dopamine modulation in the amygdala gates the selectivity of an acquired threat response, whereas inhibition of amygdala dopamine receptors is linked to threat overgeneralization.
source: Conversely, prior work suggests that dopamine modulation in the amygdala gates the selectivity of an acquired threat response, whereas inhibition of amygdala dopamine receptors is linked to threat overgeneralization (De Bundel et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement of prior findings with citation.

claim: These findings are consistent with the results that the strength of PE signaling alone does not sufficiently explain differences in learning specificity.
source: These findings are consistent with our results that the strength of PE signaling alone does not sufficiently explain differences in learning specificity.
evidence: Statement connecting prior findings to current results.

claim: The whole brain searchlight picked up state representations in other prominent cortical networks, such as the control network (lateral parietal, anterior cingulate, and dorsal lateral prefrontal regions).
source: Notably, our whole brain searchlight also picked up state representations in other prominent cortical networks, such as the control network (lateral parietal, anterior cingulate, and dorsal lateral prefrontal regions), and may accord with the possibility that distinct functional networks encode abstract state representations that vary only in format to optimize for differing task demands (Vaidya and Badre, 2022).
evidence: Statement of additional findings with citation to related theoretical work.

claim: Distinct functional networks may encode abstract state representations that vary only in format to optimize for differing task demands.
source: Notably, our whole brain searchlight also picked up state representations in other prominent cortical networks, such as the control network (lateral parietal, anterior cingulate, and dorsal lateral prefrontal regions), and may accord with the possibility that distinct functional networks encode abstract state representations that vary only in format to optimize for differing task demands (Vaidya and Badre, 2022).
evidence: Speculative statement about functional network organization with citation.

claim: The results identify a simple and domain-general neural mechanism for credit assignment in which outcomes and states are temporally bound together in the PFC.
source: To summarize, our results identify a simple and domain-general neural mechanism for credit assignment in which outcomes and states are temporally bound together in the PFC, revealing a biologically grounded model for how humans assign credit to causal cues encountered in the world.
evidence: Summary statement of main findings and their significance.

claim: How this mechanism coordinates with other known neural systems and deviates in psychiatric disorders has yet to be uncovered.
source: How this mechanism coordinates with other known neural systems and deviates in psychiatric disorders has yet to be uncovered.
evidence: Statement of future research directions.

claim: Humans and animals are thought to group action-outcome contingencies together based on causal cues that reflect states in the environment, allowing outcomes to be selectively linked to specific states.
source: In such scenarios, humans and animals are thought to group action-outcome contingencies together based on causal cues that reflect states in the environment, allowing outcomes to be selectively linked to specific states (Collins and Frank, 2013; Gershman et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement of theoretical framework with citations.

claim: Because learners have yet to discover the underlying generative structure of outcomes, and because learning and memory systems are fallible, outcomes can be misattributed and spread to irrelevant states.
source: However, because learners have yet to discover the underlying generative structure of outcomes, and because learning and memory systems are fallible, outcomes can be misattributed and spread to irrelevant states—a challenge known as the structural credit assignment problem (Hamid et al., 2021; Sutton, 1984).
evidence: Statement of theoretical problem with citations.

claim: Information gets smeared in memory which can result in overgeneralization.
source: In these cases, information gets smeared in memory (Vaidya and Fellows, 2016) which can result in overgeneralization.
evidence: Statement of consequence of credit misattribution with citation.

claim: Conventional reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms typically assume perfect credit attribution for each outcome observed.
source: While conventional reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms typically assume perfect credit attribution for each outcome observed, in reality, human learners run the gamut of how well they are able to actually assign credit.
evidence: Statement of limitation in conventional RL models.

claim: Human learners run the gamut of how well they are able to actually assign credit.
source: While conventional reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms typically assume perfect credit attribution for each outcome observed, in reality, human learners run the gamut of how well they are able to actually assign credit.
evidence: Statement of variability in human credit assignment.

claim: Discrete learning profiles can substantially shape behavior beyond the influence of classic learning parameters, such as the learning rate or the magnitude of prediction errors (PE).
source: These scenarios represent discrete learning profiles that can substantially shape behavior beyond the influence of classic learning parameters, such as the learning rate or the magnitude of prediction errors (PE).
evidence: Statement of theoretical importance of credit assignment beyond standard RL parameters.

claim: Little is currently known about how states are represented in the human brain during learning (e.g. at the stimulus level or generalized across cues), or how credit is then assigned to these specific states.
source: Little is currently known about how states are represented in the human brain during learning (e.g. at the stimulus level or generalized across cues), or how credit is then assigned to these specific states.
evidence: Statement of knowledge gap motivating the study.

claim: Non-human animal research hints that the prefrontal cortex (PFC) might play an integral role in credit assignment by binding state and action-value representations.
source: Non-human animal research hints that the prefrontal cortex (PFC) might play an integral role in credit assignment by binding state and action-value representations (Asaad et al., 2017), which could then be reinforced through midbrain dopaminergic signals to selectively gate reward attribution (O'Reilly and Frank, 2006).
evidence: Statement of prior findings from animal research with citations.

claim: State and action-value representations could be reinforced through midbrain dopaminergic signals to selectively gate reward attribution.
source: Non-human animal research hints that the prefrontal cortex (PFC) might play an integral role in credit assignment by binding state and action-value representations (Asaad et al., 2017), which could then be reinforced through midbrain dopaminergic signals to selectively gate reward attribution (O'Reilly and Frank, 2006).
evidence: Statement of theoretical mechanism with citation.

claim: Tracking state-contingent outcome history would be critical to properly assigning credit, which is believed to be governed by the lateral orbitofrontal cortex (lOFC).
source: Tracking state-contingent outcome history would also be critical to properly assigning credit, which is believed to be governed by the lateral orbitofrontal cortex (lOFC; Chau et al., 2015; Jocham et al., 2016; Walton et al., 2010).
evidence: Statement of theoretical role of lOFC with citations.

claim: Humans with lesions in the lOFC exhibit reduced state-contingent reward learning.
source: Indeed, humans with lesions in the lOFC exhibit reduced state-contingent reward learning (Noonan et al., 2017) and display a greater tendency to misattribute rewards to irrelevant causal factors (Vaidya and Fellows, 2016).
evidence: Statement of lesion study findings with citations.

claim: Humans with lesions in the lOFC display a greater tendency to misattribute rewards to irrelevant causal factors.
source: Indeed, humans with lesions in the lOFC exhibit reduced state-contingent reward learning (Noonan et al., 2017) and display a greater tendency to misattribute rewards to irrelevant causal factors (Vaidya and Fellows, 2016).
evidence: Statement of lesion study findings with citation.

claim: More recent work shows that the medial PFC and lOFC jointly track latent states by leveraging surprise signals.
source: More recent work shows that the medial PFC and lOFC jointly track latent states (Schuck et al., 2016) by leveraging surprise signals (Nassar et al., 2019), allowing for credit assignment to be performed for both experienced (Akaishi et al., 2016) and unobserved outcomes (Boorman et al., 2021; Witkowski et al., 2022).
evidence: Statement of recent findings with multiple citations.

claim: Credit assignment can be performed for both experienced and unobserved outcomes.
source: More recent work shows that the medial PFC and lOFC jointly track latent states (Schuck et al., 2016) by leveraging surprise signals (Nassar et al., 2019), allowing for credit assignment to be performed for both experienced (Akaishi et al., 2016) and unobserved outcomes (Boorman et al., 2021; Witkowski et al., 2022).
evidence: Statement of prior findings with citations.

claim: It is not known whether the configuration of neural patterns play a role in credit assignment success.
source: While prior work across species suggests that the PFC is involved in representing task states, it is not known whether the configuration of neural patterns play a role in credit assignment success.
evidence: Statement of knowledge gap.

claim: It is possible that learners actively represent task-relevant states during learning, enabling selective binding of outcomes to states in memory.
source: For example, unlike an eligibility trace, it is possible that learners actively represent task-relevant states during learning, enabling selective binding of outcomes to states in memory.
evidence: Speculative statement about potential mechanism.

claim: Allowing temporally disparate actions and outcomes to be neurally bound to the relevant state representation likely supports increased discrimination between cue-specific decision policies.
source: Allowing temporally disparate actions and outcomes to be neurally bound to the relevant state representation likely supports increased discrimination between cue-specific decision policies.
evidence: Speculative statement about functional consequence of neural binding.

claim: The precision of credit assignment may be contingent on the format and fidelity of state representations in the PFC (i.e. the degree of distinctiveness of each representation).
source: If this were the case, the precision of credit assignment may be contingent on the format and fidelity of state representations in the PFC (i.e. the degree of distinctiveness of each representation).
evidence: Speculative statement about relationship between neural representations and credit assignment.

claim: To effectively guide credit assignment, a distinct neural code representing the state when feedback is delivered should then be evoked during a subsequent related choice.
source: Thus, to effectively guide credit assignment, a distinct neural code representing the state when feedback is delivered should then be evoked during a subsequent related choice.
evidence: Speculative statement about neural mechanism for credit assignment.

claim: Failures to properly encode a state during choice or feedback should result in increased misattribution and credit spreading (i.e. attributing outcomes more diffusely to irrelevant states).
source: Failures to properly encode a state during choice or feedback should therefore result in increased misattribution and credit spreading (i.e. attributing outcomes more diffusely to irrelevant states).
evidence: Speculative statement about consequences of encoding failures.

claim: During social exchanges humans are often able to exploit social feedback to quickly learn the value of social partners.
source: For example, during social exchanges humans are often able to exploit social feedback to quickly learn the value of social partners (Lamba et al., 2020; van Baar et al., 2022), which suggests that credit may be assigned selectively to specific individuals.
evidence: Statement of prior findings with citations.

claim: Credit may be assigned selectively to specific individuals during social exchanges.
source: For example, during social exchanges humans are often able to exploit social feedback to quickly learn the value of social partners (Lamba et al., 2020; van Baar et al., 2022), which suggests that credit may be assigned selectively to specific individuals.
evidence: Inference from prior findings with citations.

claim: When learning in less familiar environments with an unknown causal structure (e.g. gambling with slot machines) learners may assign credit less precisely by spreading credit across states.
source: In contrast, when learning in less familiar environments with an unknown causal structure (e.g. gambling with slot machines) learners may assign credit less precisely by spreading credit across states.
evidence: Speculative statement about credit assignment in nonsocial contexts.

claim: Prior work suggests that humans differ in how they strategically use feedback when learning about social partners compared to learning about reward-matched bandits.
source: Prior work also suggests that humans differ in how they strategically use feedback when learning about social partners compared to learning about reward-matched bandits (Chang et al., 2010; Lamba et al., 2020), providing an ideal empirical setup to probe for differences and commonalities in credit assignment precision across contexts.
evidence: Statement of prior findings with citations justifying experimental design.

claim: Different learning profiles are due to how precisely individuals assign credit, with some participants consistently spreading credit, particularly when gambling and after a negative outcome.
source: We find that different learning profiles are due to how precisely individuals assign credit, with some participants consistently spreading credit, particularly when gambling and after a negative outcome.
evidence: Summary statement of main behavioral findings.

claim: Multivariate neural patterns in prefrontal regions, including the lOFC and mPFC, encode state representations, but do so less precisely in those who spread credit.
source: Multivariate neural patterns in prefrontal regions, including the lOFC and mPFC, encode state representations, but do so less precisely in those who spread credit.
evidence: Summary statement of main neural findings.

claim: High-fidelity state representations were associated with greater task earnings and more precise credit assignment—an effect that could not be explained by learning rate or the strength of the PE.
source: Indeed, high-fidelity state representations were associated with greater task earnings and more precise credit assignment—an effect that could not be explained by learning rate or the strength of the PE.
evidence: Summary statement of main findings ruling out alternative explanations.

claim: Precise credit assignment is achieved through neural state representations sharing a common geometry across choice and feedback, signifying a persistent neural code indexing a stimulus' identity.
source: Precise credit assignment is achieved through neural state representations sharing a common geometry across choice and feedback, signifying a persistent neural code indexing a stimulus' identity.
evidence: Summary statement of main mechanistic finding.

claim: Participants credit task-relevant cues more precisely in social compared to nonsocial contexts, a process that is mediated by high-fidelity (i.e., distinct and consistent) state representations in the PFC.
source: Participants credit task-relevant cues more precisely in social compared to nonsocial contexts, a process that is mediated by high-fidelity (i.e., distinct and consistent) state representations in the PFC.
evidence: Summary statement from abstract of main findings.

claim: The medial PFC and orbitofrontal cortex work in concert to match the neural codes from feedback to those at choice, and the strength of these common neural codes predicts credit assignment precision.
source: Specifically, the medial PFC and orbitofrontal cortex work in concert to match the neural codes from feedback to those at choice, and the strength of these common neural codes predicts credit assignment precision.
evidence: Summary statement from abstract of main mechanistic finding.
